frameworks.name: Triangle Framework for Non-Performance
frameworks.definition: A three-vertex diagnostic tool (adapted from Andy Grove and Layla Hormozi) that isolates the root cause of any employee non-performance: (1) they don't know the expectation was set, (2) they don't know how to perform it, or (3) they are not motivated to perform it.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that there are exactly three reasons any employee fails to do what a manager wants: they were never told the expectation clearly, they were not trained in how to do it, or they lack the motivation or incentive to do it. Andy Grove's High Output Management named only two (can't do / won't do); Hormozi added the third (doesn't know it's expected) after encountering real situations where neither Grove category applied.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to any employee, manager, or individual contributor role
within a company the manager controls
bounded_by: Andy Grove's original two-reason model (can't / won't) is incomplete — a third category (doesn't know) is missing from Grove's framing

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the reporting cadence around a metric or task is the strongest implicit signal of its importance: if a manager asks for a metric daily or twice daily, employees perceive it as critical; if it appears once per quarter on a slide, they treat it as minor; if it is never reported on, they effectively consider it irrelevant and will almost certainly not perform it.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies across all employee levels and company sizes
claims.mechanism: Frequency of requested reporting acts as an implicit priority signal — the faster the cadence, the more important the employee infers the task to be, which drives compliance.

anchors.value: employee perceives as very high priority

anchors.region: once per quarter, single line item on a slide

anchors.value: employee almost certainly will not do it

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that communicating an expectation once is insufficient; effective expectation-setting requires (a) verbal communication, (b) repetition of that communication, and (c) written documentation in multiple places, ideally embedded into daily or weekly checklists or reporting structures.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies whenever a manager wants a task or standard performed consistently

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that businesses plateau when they stop applying at scale the basics that drove early success — specifically the high-touch personal service and frequent interaction that characterized the early stage — and that being advanced simply means consistently performing the basics even at high volume, not adding complexity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service businesses that grew via founder-led personal delivery
businesses that have begun hiring to replace founder involvement
claims.mechanism: When founders hire, service quality degrades because employees replicate neither the skill nor the personal investment of the founder; the business stopped doing the basics at scale.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that when diagnosing an underperforming employee it is more effective to protect their ego by framing the gap as atypical of their behavior (e.g., 'it's really unlike you to be late for stuff') before asking what is causing it, rather than leading with criticism of their character or competence.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: direct conversation between manager and underperforming employee
employee is someone the manager values and wants to retain
claims.mechanism: Leading with an embedded compliment (it's unlike you to fail) protects the employee's ego while still targeting the behavior, making the conversation less defensive and more productive.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that if compensation is structured around four activities and a fifth activity is added without compensation adjustment, the employee will almost certainly deprioritize the fifth activity regardless of how important the manager states it is.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: employee whose compensation is tied to specific deliverables or metrics
manager adds new responsibilities outside the existing compensation scope
claims.mechanism: Compensation structure acts as a revealed-preference signal — employees allocate discretionary effort toward compensated activities and away from uncompensated ones regardless of stated priority.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that employees who understand the purpose behind a requested activity are substantially more likely to perform it consistently than employees who are given instructions without context, because purposeless activity feels like prison-camp labor — arbitrary and demoralizing.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies particularly to repetitive administrative tasks (e.g., CRM note entry) where the benefit accrues to a downstream team, not the performer
claims.mechanism: When an employee understands how their specific action benefits the downstream team and ideally themselves (e.g., better-qualified leads raise their own close rate), they internalize the motivation rather than treating the task as imposed busywork.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that explaining the personal benefit to the employee — not just the organizational benefit — of completing a task substantially increases the likelihood of compliance, because while some employees respond to team-level rationale, many primarily act on personal incentives.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: when assigning tasks whose direct benefit accrues to the organization or another team
with employees who are individually oriented rather than team-mission oriented
claims.mechanism: Personal benefit framing converts abstract organizational goals into concrete individual gain (e.g., better CRM notes → better-screened leads → higher close rate for that rep → more commission), making the motivation intrinsic rather than imposed.
bounded_by: Some employees ('good people') will act on organizational benefit alone; personal framing is the fallback for those who will not

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that after the triangle framework has been applied — expectation communicated, training given, incentive aligned — and an employee still fails to perform, the conversation should shift explicitly to whether the role is right for the person, and that reassigning to a different role within the company is often preferable to termination if the person is a cultural fit with other useful skills.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: employee has been given clear expectation, training, and aligned incentive
employee remains a cultural fit with other demonstrated skills
bounded_by: Hormozi notes nine times out of ten the other role fit is not the right call — the manager should hire the person they would normally hire for the open role rather than defaulting to reassigning an underperformer with a history of failure in the current role

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that training an employee must include not only how to perform the task but also how to manage their schedule to make room for the new task alongside existing responsibilities, because time management incapacity is often misdiagnosed as motivational failure.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: when adding new responsibilities to an existing employee who is already at capacity

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that when an employee cites being too busy as the reason for non-performance, managers should consider whether it is a motivation deficit (if given $10,000 as an incentive they would find time) or a training deficit (they genuinely lack the scheduling skill to fit in the activity), rather than accepting the face-value excuse.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: employee who claims busyness rather than unwillingness
claims.mechanism: The $10,000 hypothetical tests whether time is actually the constraint: if sufficient incentive would free up time, the real constraint is motivation, not capacity.

examples.text: Alex Hormozi describes hiring a new sales manager he was excited about. A few weeks in, Hormozi confronted the manager about not having done any call reviews. The manager replied that he was unaware call reviews were expected. Hormozi acknowledges he had assumed call reviews were an obvious part of a sales director role — but had never explicitly communicated that expectation. This example illustrates the first vertex of the triangle: employees don't do things because the expectation was never communicated, even when it seems obvious to the manager.

Alex Hormozi gives a concrete CRM-note example to illustrate purpose-driven compliance. He walks through why a sales rep entering detailed call notes benefits finance (better collection conversations), customer success (more personalized onboarding), and most directly the rep themselves (better-screened leads on the front end, raising their own close rate and reducing time wasted on tire kickers). The example demonstrates how explaining downstream benefit — especially personal benefit — converts a perceived administrative burden into a self-interested routine.

Alex Hormozi describes a small business growth pattern: in the early stage, founders grow by providing high personal interaction and excellent service. When they hire teammates, service quality drops because fewer smiles, less skill, and less personal attention are in play. He frames this as the business stopping the basics at scale — and says it explains why most small businesses plateau. The example illustrates that being advanced is not complexity; it is consistently doing what worked early, at higher volume.

practices.text: When diagnosing an underperforming employee, ask them directly: did I not communicate the expectation clearly? Do you not know how to do it? Are you not motivated to do it? Give them the three boxes and let them self-diagnose, which isolates the root cause and depersonalizes the conversation.

When onboarding a new hire into a task or responsibility, show them how to do it, document the process in writing (ideally recorded), and specify exactly how they should report completion back to you so you know it was done.

Make sure every important task or metric is measured and reported on a frequent basis — weekly at minimum, daily for critical items. If you never ask for it in reporting, employees will infer it is unimportant.

Before concluding an employee is unmotivated, verify their compensation structure actually rewards the task you are asking them to perform. If the task is outside their existing comp scope, adjust compensation or incentives before escalating the performance conversation.

When explaining a new task to an employee, always explain both the organizational why (how it helps the team or company) and the personal why (how it specifically benefits the employee's own performance or earnings).
